title: Easter is fifty days
hookLine: Christ is risen! He is risen indeed! Orthodox Pascha often falls on a later date, by the old calendar

cards: Midnight, outside an Orthodox church. Hundreds of people holding candles in the street, some of them kids way past bedtime. The priest steps out and calls, Christ is risen!
In a Greek church, Christos anesti. The whole crowd shouts back: Truly he is risen! Again, and again, louder.
Then fireworks, bells, and people kissing each other three times on the cheek. For weeks afterward, friends greet each other that way on the street, even in text messages.

In English-speaking churches you'll hear: Christ is risen! He is risen indeed! It all goes back to a Sunday morning, and some women at an empty tomb, where an angel says, "He is not here: for he is risen, as he said."

teach.b: Pascha, the Greek and Latin name for Easter, comes from the Hebrew Pesach, Passover.

Jesus died and rose at Passover time, and the first Christians, who were Jewish, heard his death and rising as a new passing over, from death to life. Paul writes: "Christ our passover is sacrificed for us."
So in French, Easter is Pâques; in Spanish, Pascua. English says Easter, a word whose origin is still debated.
The English reply echoes Luke: when two disciples rush back to Jerusalem, the others meet them with the news, "The Lord is risen indeed."

teach.h: THE FULL MOON AND TWO CALENDARS.
teach.b: Western churches keep Easter on the Sunday after the first full moon of spring, by their reckoning.

Orthodox churches count by the older Julian calendar, so Orthodox Pascha often falls later, sometimes by weeks, and some years both land on the same day. Families with a foot in both traditions sometimes celebrate twice.
And Easter isn't only a day.
Like Christmas, it's a season, and a longer one: fifty days, all the way to Pentecost, with the candles burning and the alleluias going. For Christians, this is the center of everything.
Paul put it bluntly: "And if Christ be not risen, then is our preaching vain, and your faith is also vain." That's the weight behind the shout.

how: Christians celebrate Easter, or Pascha, with services at dawn, at the vigil or at midnight, greeting one another with Christ is risen and the reply He is risen indeed; many churches keep the Easter season for fifty days, to Pentecost.

games.q: you're one of the women at the tomb. the stone is rolled away, and an angel says he is not here, for he is risen. what do you do?
o: stay at the tomb to be sure.
run to tell the disciples, afraid and overjoyed.
go home and tell no one.
games.why: in Matthew they leave "with fear and great joy" and run to tell. Mark's ending says they were afraid and said nothing, at least at first.

practice: Think of the women running from the tomb, scared and overjoyed at once, with news they could barely say.
Then bring to mind one piece of good news, yours or someone else's, that deserves telling: a recovery, a new job, a kindness someone doesn't know about, and picture the person who should hear it.
If you pray, give thanks for it; if you don't, just hold it for a moment.
